promptText: Why does a Kafka consumer group's parallelism have a hard ceiling at the topic's partition count, no matter how many consumer instances you add?
options: Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer within a group; adding consumers beyond the partition count leaves the extra instances with no partition to read, so they add no throughput at all
Kafka charges a per-instance licensing fee that discourages scaling consumers beyond the partition count
Every partition can already be read concurrently by unlimited consumers within the same group, so no such ceiling actually exists
Consumer count is capped by the number of ZooKeeper nodes present in every Kafka deployment, including KRaft-mode clusters
explanation: Kafka's ordinary consumer-group mechanics assign each partition to exactly one consumer in a group, so partition count is a capacity decision made up front - extra consumers beyond it sit idle with no partition assigned.

promptText: What is the fundamental behavioral difference between a point-to-point queue and Kafka's event streaming model regarding message retention?
options: A queue deletes a message once a consumer has processed it; Kafka retains the message in its durable log per a retention policy, allowing replay by resetting a consumer group's offset
Kafka deletes every message immediately after any single consumer group finishes reading it
Queues retain messages indefinitely by default, while Kafka deletes messages immediately upon publish
Both models delete messages in exactly the same way; the only real difference is the client library's API surface
explanation: The chapter's crisp one-liner: a queue deletes a message after one consumer handles it, while a stream keeps the whole ordered log so that data is a re-readable source of truth - the consumer owns its offset, not the broker.

promptText: Why does committing/acking a message AFTER successful processing (rather than before) give you at-least-once rather than at-most-once delivery?
options: If the consumer crashes after processing but before committing, the message is redelivered on restart since the commit never happened - so a message may be processed more than once, but it can never be silently lost
Acking after processing guarantees a message is processed exactly once with absolutely no possibility of duplication
The order in which processing and acking happen has no effect on delivery guarantees in any messaging system
Acking after processing always causes the message to be permanently lost if the consumer happens to restart
explanation: The chapter defines at-least-once precisely this way: committing after processing means a crash in that window causes reprocessing on restart, never silent loss - which is exactly why idempotency matters under this, the default and most common guarantee.

promptText: In RabbitMQ's AMQP model, why do producers publish to an exchange rather than directly to a queue?
options: The exchange evaluates bindings and routing keys to decide which queue(s) receive a copy, which is exactly what gives RabbitMQ its flexible routing (direct/topic/fanout) that publishing straight to a queue could not provide
Publishing directly to a queue is technically impossible under any version of the AMQP protocol
Exchanges exist purely to handle authentication and have no effect on where a message is actually routed
Exchanges are a Kafka-specific concept and do not actually exist in RabbitMQ's architecture
explanation: The chapter's mental model: RabbitMQ is a router that pushes messages into queues via this exchange-then-binding indirection, which is precisely what makes direct/topic/fanout routing possible - a producer never targets a queue directly.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers over chasing true end-to-end exactly-once semantics?
options: Kafka's exactly-once guarantees (idempotent producers, transactions) only hold within Kafka itself; the moment a consumer's side effect touches an external system (charging a card, sending an email), that action and the offset commit are not naturally atomic across the network, so at-least-once plus idempotency is the practical, achievable target
Exactly-once semantics are fully achievable end-to-end in every case, and the chapter recommends it as the universal default
At-least-once delivery on its own already guarantees that no message is ever processed more than once
Idempotent consumers are a concept that only matters when using RabbitMQ, never when using Kafka
explanation: The chapter's winning line: aim for at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers, which gives effectively-once processing without the cost and limits of true exactly-once - Kafka's exactly-once is real, but only end-to-end within Kafka itself.

promptText: What distinguishes a "poison message" from a merely transient failure, and how should each be handled?
options: A poison message can never be processed successfully (a permanent bug or malformed payload), so retrying it forever would block the queue/partition and starve everything behind it - it should be routed to a Dead Letter Queue after the retry budget is exhausted, while transient failures should be retried with backoff
A poison message should always be retried indefinitely until the underlying bug is eventually fixed in production
The only correct response to any poison message is to silently drop it with no logging or dead-lettering at all
Poison messages resolve themselves automatically after a fixed 24-hour period with no other handling required
explanation: The chapter's core distinction: retry the transient failures with exponential backoff, and dead-letter the permanent ones - blindly retrying a poison message forever blocks the partition/queue and starves every message behind it.

promptText: A team needs every event for a given order processed strictly in sequence, while still wanting horizontal scalability across the whole topic. How does choosing the partition key resolve this, and what do they give up?
options: Using the order id as the partition key routes all of that order's events to the same partition, guaranteeing per-key ordering, while different orders' events land on different partitions and are processed in parallel - global ordering across all orders is not guaranteed, but that is the accepted trade-off for scalability
Choosing any partition key guarantees both global ordering and unlimited parallelism simultaneously with no trade-off at all
Ordering can only be guaranteed by routing the entire topic through a single partition, and the partition key has no effect on ordering
The partition key only determines which broker physically stores the data and has no bearing on ordering behavior
explanation: The chapter's framing: 'order by key, not globally' - keying on the entity whose events must stay sequenced gives per-key ordering while unrelated entities process concurrently; demanding total ordering forces a single partition and destroys parallelism.

promptText: What is the throughput-vs-fairness trade-off of setting RabbitMQ's consumer prefetch count very high (e.g. 250) versus very low (e.g. 1)?
options: A high prefetch lets a consumer pull a large batch and process it without per-message network round trips, raising throughput, but a crash mid-batch redelivers the entire unacked batch at once and can starve other competing consumers of work; a low prefetch keeps distribution fair and bounds crash blast-radius at the cost of a round trip per message
Prefetch count only affects message ordering guarantees and has no bearing on throughput at all
A prefetch of 1 always produces strictly higher throughput than any higher prefetch value in every scenario
A high prefetch count guarantees strict message ordering across all competing consumers on the queue
explanation: The chapter frames prefetch as a genuine throughput-vs-fairness knob: low prefetch (as low as 1) keeps distribution even with minimal redelivery blast radius on crash, while high prefetch trades that fairness and blast-radius safety for batched, higher throughput.

promptText: Why did RabbitMQ replace classic mirrored queues with quorum queues, and what consensus mechanism powers the replacement?
options: Classic mirrored queues could silently lose unacknowledged messages or briefly accept writes on two mirrors during certain network-partition/failover scenarios, since their replication was never fully consistent; quorum queues use the Raft protocol, requiring a majority of replicas to persist a write before it's acknowledged, giving a provable consistency guarantee
Quorum queues were introduced purely to improve raw message throughput, with no implications for consistency or data safety
Classic mirrored queues remain the recommended default for replication in RabbitMQ 4.0, with quorum queues reserved only for niche use cases
Quorum queues rely on a two-phase commit protocol rather than any leader-election-based consensus mechanism
explanation: The chapter is explicit: classic mirroring gave availability without a rigorous consistency proof and could lose messages under partition/failover; quorum queues apply Raft's majority-write guarantee - the same fundamental idea as Kafka's ISR-based leader election - and are now the only supported HA option in RabbitMQ 4.0.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend pairing RabbitMQ's publisher confirms with the `mandatory` flag and a `basic.return` handler, rather than relying on confirms alone?
options: A confirm only tells you the broker received and persisted the message; it does NOT tell you the message was actually routed anywhere - an unroutable message (no matching queue bound) can still be confirmed by the exchange yet silently dropped unless `mandatory` triggers a `basic.return` back to the producer
Publisher confirms and the mandatory/basic.return mechanism are functionally redundant, and either one alone is fully sufficient on its own
Confirms only apply to consumer-side acknowledgements and have no relationship to producer-side delivery tracking whatsoever
The mandatory flag is required before RabbitMQ will accept any published message under any configuration
explanation: The chapter's precise line: confirms tell you the broker got it, mandatory-plus-returns tells you it actually went somewhere - a message can be confirmed received by the exchange yet still be unroutable, which a confirm alone would never reveal.

promptText: Why is an SQS queue typically placed behind each SNS subscription in the fan-out pattern, rather than having each consumer subscribe to SNS directly?
options: SNS itself has no durable retention: it retries push delivery to an unavailable subscriber only for a bounded period and then drops the message; an SQS queue in between gives each consumer its own durable buffer, independent consumption rate, and its own DLQ
SNS is architecturally incapable of delivering a message to more than one subscriber unless an SQS queue sits in front of each one
SQS is a mandatory AWS prerequisite service that must exist before any SNS topic can be created at all
SNS messages are internally converted into Kafka topics, which requires an SQS queue as a translation layer
explanation: The chapter states the durability reasoning explicitly: SNS alone can drop a message for an unavailable subscriber once its own retry window expires; SNS-to-SQS fan-out gives every subscriber its own durable, independently-paced buffer instead.

promptText: Standard SQS queues offer nearly unlimited throughput with best-effort ordering, while FIFO queues guarantee strict ordering. What is the actual mechanism and cost of that FIFO guarantee?
options: FIFO orders and deduplicates strictly within a MessageGroupId (conceptually like a Kafka partition key), capping throughput at roughly 300 messages/second unbatched (about 3,000/second batched) - far below a standard queue's effectively unbounded rate
FIFO queues guarantee global ordering across all message groups simultaneously with no throughput penalty compared to Standard queues
Standard queues already guarantee strict ordering as long as the application uses only a single consumer
FIFO queues achieve ordering purely through client-side sorting logic after receipt, with no broker-side mechanism involved at all
explanation: The chapter's decision rule ties ordering directly to a real throughput cost: FIFO's strict per-group ordering and dedup come at roughly 300-3,000 msgs/sec, a steep drop from Standard's effectively unbounded rate - choose FIFO only when correctness of order/dedup matters more than raw volume.

promptText: What is the "dual-write problem," and precisely how does the transactional outbox pattern fix it without requiring a distributed transaction across the database and the broker?
options: Writing to the database and separately publishing an event are two different systems that cannot be committed atomically; the outbox pattern writes the event as a row in an outbox table inside the SAME local database transaction as the business change, so both commit or roll back together via ordinary ACID guarantees, and a separate relay/CDC process then reliably publishes each outbox row to the broker afterward
The outbox pattern solves this by wrapping the database write and the broker publish inside a single two-phase commit transaction spanning both systems
The dual-write problem only ever arises when using Kafka specifically, and does not apply to RabbitMQ or SQS as message destinations
The outbox pattern requires the message broker itself to natively support ACID transactions across every participating service
explanation: The chapter is precise here: no plain built-in mechanism commits a DB write and a broker publish atomically across two systems; outbox sidesteps this entirely by keeping both the business change and the event write inside one local ACID transaction, then relaying afterward - broker-agnostic by construction.

promptText: During a rolling deploy, why must a genuinely breaking message schema change be rolled out consumer-first, then producer, then a cleanup deploy - never producer-first or all-at-once?
options: Old and new versions of producers/consumers inevitably run simultaneously for some window; if the producer starts emitting the new shape before consumers can handle it, in-flight old consumers fail to deserialize new messages, and a backlog of old-shape messages can outlive the deploy itself - so consumers must support both shapes before the producer ever emits the new one, with cleanup deferred until the backlog is confirmed drained
Message brokers automatically buffer every in-flight message until all service instances are running the exact same version, making rollout order irrelevant
Producer-first rollout is always safe as long as the entire deploy completes within a five-minute window
Schema-change rollout ordering only matters for Kafka-based systems; RabbitMQ and SQS deployments have no equivalent risk
explanation: The chapter's safe ordering exists precisely because rolling deploys are never instantaneous across every instance: consumers must be able to handle both shapes before the producer changes, and cleanup must wait until the old-shape backlog has genuinely drained, not merely until the deploy finished.

promptText: Applying Little's Law to size a competing-consumers fleet: if a single message takes 2 seconds to process (T) and the system must sustain 50 messages/second (R), roughly how many concurrent consumers are needed just to keep the backlog from growing, and what two ceilings can still cap this regardless of the math?
options: Roughly R x T = 100 concurrent consumers; but Kafka consumer count beyond the partition count adds nothing, and RabbitMQ/SQS consumer count can keep climbing yet eventually saturate a shared downstream resource (a DB connection pool, a rate-limited API), at which point adding more consumers stops helping or even hurts via contention
Exactly 2 consumers are needed regardless of throughput requirements, since T alone determines the necessary concurrency
Exactly 50 consumers are needed because R alone determines concurrency, with T having no bearing on the calculation at all
There is no principled way to estimate the required consumer count; it can only be discovered empirically through a production incident
explanation: The chapter names Little's Law explicitly (concurrency needed is roughly throughput times per-item latency) as the way to reason about sizing with real numbers, while also flagging the two hard ceilings - partition count and shared downstream capacity - that no amount of added consumers can push past.
